text: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
context_note: From the Sermon on the Mount, on oaths: plain, reliable speech is commanded so that truthfulness needs no reinforcement. It grounds the broad Christian presumption against deceit.

text: And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them. Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.
context_note: The Hebrew midwives deceive Pharaoh to save newborn boys and are blessed. A standing puzzle for absolute prohibitions of lying, discussed since Augustine.

text: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
context_note: Vows are voluntary but, once made, binding; the text prefers restraint in promising to failure in performing.

text: He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
context_note: Part of a psalm describing who may dwell with God: the faithful person keeps a sworn word even when keeping it has become costly.

text: Thou shalt not kill.
context_note: The sixth commandment. The Hebrew verb targets unlawful killing; the tradition has always read it alongside provisions for defense, war, and judicial punishment.

text: Nothing hinders one act from having two effects, only one of which is intended, while the other is beside the intention.
context_note: Aquinas's discussion of killing in self-defense, the classical source of the doctrine of double effect: defending one's life is licit though death of the aggressor results, provided the death is not intended.

text: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
context_note: The non-resistance saying that grounds Christian pacifism; traditions differ on whether it binds private persons absolutely or states at all.

text: For it is the wrongdoing of the opposing party which compels the wise man to wage just wars; and this wrong-doing, even though it gave rise to no war, would still be matter of grief to man because it is man's wrong-doing.
context_note: Augustine concedes that wars may be just while insisting they remain occasions of grief; the passage seeds the just-war tradition's reluctant permission rather than celebration of war.

text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
context_note: A beatitude blessing those who make peace; cited across Christian history against easy recourse to arms.

text: For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
context_note: Paul on the magistrate's sword, historically the key text for state authority to punish, including capitally; modern readings dispute how far the sword extends.

text: So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
context_note: Jesus halts a lawful execution by turning scrutiny on the executioners; a central text for mercy limiting punishment.

text: It is not without significance, that in no passage of the holy canonical books there can be found either divine precept or permission to take away our own life, whether for the sake of entering on the enjoyment of immortality, or of shunning or ridding ourselves of anything whatever.
context_note: Augustine's argument, against admiration of Roman suicides, that scripture nowhere permits taking one's own life; it fixed the mainline Christian position.

text: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
context_note: Paul's claim that the body is not one's own possession; cited in Christian discussion of self-harm and of what may be done with one's life.

text: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
context_note: Job's response to catastrophic loss; in end-of-life discussion it frames life's beginning and end as in God's hands rather than ours.

text: Wherefore suicide is always a mortal sin, as being contrary to the natural law and to charity.
context_note: Aquinas's conclusion that taking one's own life offends against self-love, community, and God's dominion; later Catholic teaching distinguishes this from declining disproportionate treatment.

text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
context_note: From the Sermon on the Mount: accumulation is spiritually dangerous because the heart follows the treasure; the standing charter for Christian detachment from wealth.

text: I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
context_note: Paul's farewell at Miletus, preserving a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels; giving is presented as blessing rather than loss.

text: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
context_note: Riches are not condemned outright here: the wealthy are charged to hold wealth without trust in it and to give readily — a counterweight to purely renunciant readings.

text: Thou shalt not steal.
context_note: The eighth commandment, the fixed point of biblical property ethics; the tradition debates its edges, not its center.

text: It is not theft, properly speaking, to take secretly and use another's property in a case of extreme need: because that which he takes for the support of his life becomes his own property by reason of that need.
context_note: Aquinas's teaching that in extreme necessity all things are common: taking bread to survive is not theft at all, rather than excused theft. It marks the limit of the property right, not a license.

text: But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
context_note: Lending without expectation of return, set inside love of enemies; the verse anchored centuries of Christian usury prohibition.

text: To take usury for money lent is unjust in itself, because this is to sell what does not exist, and this evidently leads to inequality which is contrary to justice.
context_note: Aquinas's core argument against usury: money is consumed in use, so charging for its use sells nothing. Later casuistry admitted extrinsic titles, and modern teaching tolerates moderate interest.

text: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
context_note: Attached to the Lord's Prayer: divine forgiveness is bound to the disciple's forgiveness of others, making forgiveness a requirement rather than a counsel.

text: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
context_note: Retaliation is surrendered to God's justice; the verse separates renouncing private revenge from denying that wrongs matter.

text: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
context_note: The fifth commandment, the only one carrying a promise; honor here includes material support of aged parents, as later teaching makes explicit.

text: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
context_note: Written about support of widowed family members: providing for one's household, parents included, is treated as a test of faith itself.

text: If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.
context_note: A hard saying relativizing family bonds before discipleship; read with the fifth commandment it shows filial duty is weighty but not ultimate.

text: Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
context_note: Jesus grounds marriage in creation rather than contract; the one-flesh union is the basis of both the fidelity demand and the divorce teaching.

text: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
context_note: Fidelity is interiorized: the Sermon on the Mount moves adultery from act to intention, making the guarding of desire part of faithfulness.

text: He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so. And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.
context_note: Jesus treats the Mosaic divorce provision as concession, not ideal, while the exception clause became the crux of Christian divorce doctrine and its denominational splits.

text: But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.
context_note: The Pauline concession for marriages abandoned by an unbelieving spouse; churches differ over how far this 'privilege' extends the grounds for divorce.

text: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
context_note: Alluding to Abraham's visitors at Mamre: the stranger at the door may bear God's presence, so hospitality is watchfulness, not charity from surplus.

text: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
context_note: From the judgment scene: welcome given to the stranger is received by Christ himself, which makes hospitality a matter on which one is finally judged.

text: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
context_note: The proverb treats pride less as rule-breaking than as self-deception that precedes ruin; humility is realism about one's standing before God.

text: For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
context_note: Spoken at a banquet about seat-taking: the reversal of self-exaltation is a fixed pattern in Jesus's teaching.

text: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
context_note: The tenth commandment uniquely legislates desire rather than act, placing envy itself under the law.

text: Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
context_note: Paul writes from prison that contentment is learned, not circumstantial; the Christian answer to envy is trained gratitude.

text: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
context_note: The classic charter of Christian political obedience; its scope has been contested wherever rulers commanded what God forbids.

text: Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
context_note: The apostles before the council: the standing exception to Romans 13, invoked by conscientious resisters throughout Christian history.

text: Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
context_note: The most quoted verse on judgment; in context it targets hypocritical judgment (the mote and the beam follow), not moral discernment as such.

text: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
context_note: Jesus commands right judgment rather than none; held together with Matthew 7 it yields the traditional distinction between condemnation and discernment.
